c1-01: Sweden stretches about 1,600 km from Treriksröset in the north to Smygehuk in the south.
c1-02: The Baltic Sea lies to the east. On the west coast are Skagerrak and Kattegat.
c1-03: Warm water heats the air, and winds carry the milder, damper air over Sweden.
c1-04: Vänern, Vättern and Mälaren are Sweden's three largest lakes. Öland and Gotland are islands, and Kattegat is a sea.
c1-05: 290 municipalities, 21 counties, 25 provinces and 349 members of the Riksdag. These four numbers are often mixed up.
c1-06: Norrland is in the north, Svealand in the middle and Götaland in the south. Bohuslän is a province, not one of the three main parts.
c1-07: Sweden has almost 11 million people, and about 85 percent live in cities.
c1-08: Kiruna and Malmberget are in Norrbotten, and the ore is shipped onward by train.
c1-09: 2045 is the target in the Swedish Climate Act (klimatlagen). Don't confuse it with the EU's target for 2050.
c1-10: Smygehuk is Sweden's southernmost point, at the opposite end of the country from Treriksröset (the northernmost point). Kebnekaise is the highest mountain, and Malmberget is a mining town in Norrbotten — neither marks the country's extreme points.
c1-11: Norden consists of five countries: Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland are neighboring countries, but are not part of Norden.
c1-12: The North Atlantic Current carries the Gulf Stream's warm water onward across the Atlantic toward Europe. The other currents are real, but flow along the coasts of North or South America or Africa, not Scandinavia.
c1-13: As the ice melted it shaped the landscape — many lakes, archipelagos with thousands of islands, and plains with fertile soil. The mild climate is due to warm ocean currents, not the ice age, and the division into counties and the move to cities are administrative and social processes from a much later era, unrelated to the ice age.
c1-14: Kebnekaise reaches about 2,000 meters. That is noticeably lower than mountains of 3,000 meters and above, such as in the Alps, but still much higher than the hilly landscape of southern Sweden.
c1-15: In the mountains the climate is too cold and windy for trees to grow — the landscape consists mostly of rock, grass and low plants. The right of public access does not prevent planting trees, industrial logging happens in other parts of the country, and the mountains are of course above sea level, not below.
c1-16: Forest covers more than half of Sweden's land area. That is noticeably more than a quarter or a tenth, but not 'almost the entire area' — the rest is taken up by lakes, mountains, farmland and cities.
c1-17: In the cold north, conifers such as spruce and pine dominate, while broadleaf trees are more common in the milder southern areas. The reverse pattern and 'the same forest everywhere' do not reflect reality — the climate changes from north to south.
c1-18: A sea area near the coast with many closely spaced islands is called an archipelago (skärgård). Fjäll is mountainous terrain, landskap is a historical region, and kommun is an administrative unit — none of them describes a cluster of islands at sea.
c1-19: Sweden has around 250,000 islands — more than any other country in the world. Norway and Finland also have plenty of islands and archipelagos, but do not surpass Sweden in number.
c1-20: Sweden is divided into 25 provinces. 21 is the number of counties, 290 the number of municipalities, and 349 the number of members of the Riksdag — these four numbers are often mixed up.
c1-21: The provinces used to have their own laws, but today play no administrative role in how Sweden is governed — even so, many Swedes still feel a connection to the province where they were born or live. Healthcare is run by the regions, taxes are set by municipalities and regions, and the provinces have no government of their own.
c1-22: Sweden's three largest cities are Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö — around four million people live in and around them. Uppsala, Lund and Norrköping are also real Swedish cities, but noticeably smaller.
c1-23: Sweden's population is not evenly distributed — most people live in the southern part of the country and along the coasts, so northern Sweden is the least populated. Stockholm, Gothenburg and Skåne, on the contrary, are among the most densely populated regions.
c1-24: Besides iron ore, copper, zinc, lead and gold are also mined in Swedish mines. Coal, oil, natural gas, diamonds, platinum, salt and limestone are not mentioned as products of these mines.
c1-25: Iron and steel have long been an important part of the Swedish economy — not a recent 21st-century phenomenon, and not a minor product for a single neighboring country, since the products are exported to many countries.
c1-26: Besides as drinking water, water in Sweden is used in agriculture and industry, as well as an energy source for hydropower. Shipping, fishing and tourism do occur but are not the main categories of use described here.
c1-27: A hydropower plant uses the energy of flowing water to produce electricity — hydropower accounts for a large share of Sweden's electricity production. Purifying drinking water, irrigating fields and regulating fish stocks are not among its functions.
c1-28: Most of Sweden's agriculture is concentrated in southern Sweden, where the climate is milder and more favorable for farming. In the north, in the mountains and at high elevations, the climate is too cold for large-scale farming.
c1-29: Sweden's forest industry produces pulp, paper, cardboard and timber for the construction industry — these products are exported to many countries. Christmas trees for export, car fuel and furniture only for the domestic market do not reflect the industry's real scale.
c1-30: The main cause is human emissions of greenhouse gases from transport, industry and agriculture. Solar activity and volcanoes do affect the climate, but are not considered the main cause of today's accelerated warming; meanwhile the oceans are warming, not cooling.
c1-31: More frequent heavy downpours and the resulting floods are a direct consequence of climate change, which is expected to become more common in Sweden. Sweden has not abandoned the Climate Act's target, sea levels are rising due to warming rather than falling, and the phenomenon is clearly linked to climate.
c1-32: The target means that Sweden should not emit more greenhouse gases than nature can absorb. It is not a total ban on cars or giving up electricity, and it is a Swedish national target — the EU has its own target for 2050.
c1-33: Sustainable development means using natural resources so that future generations can also live well, and states, companies and individuals can all contribute — not only the state, and not only rich countries. It is not about giving up resources entirely, but about using them responsibly.
c1-34: Taking public transport, saving electricity and sorting waste for recycling are concrete ways to reduce climate impact in everyday life. Driving unnecessarily, avoiding recycling and burning trash at home, on the contrary, increase the burden on the environment.
c2-01: The word comes from Greek and means rule by the people.
c2-02: Everyone votes behind a screen in a voting booth so no one else sees their choice.
c2-03: The rule of law (rättssäkerhet) also means that the laws apply equally to everyone in Sweden.
c2-04: You can exert influence by voting, contacting politicians, demonstrating, signing petitions, and submitting views to the municipality.
c2-05: Low voter turnout can in turn widen the gaps between different groups in society.
c2-06: Integration means that people with different backgrounds live closer to each other and feel part of society. The first option describes the opposite concept — segregation.
c2-07: In a democracy, those who hold power should be replaceable — for example, at the next election. Holding on to power forever, concentrating it in a single person, or passing it down within one family go against the very idea of democracy.
c2-08: Yes — everyone has the right not to take part in an election, voting is not mandatory in Sweden, and there are no fines for not voting. There is no requirement to give written notice in advance that you are abstaining.
c2-09: Free elections mean that there must be several parties to choose between, that everyone can vote without threats or coercion, and that everyone has one vote. The right to vote is not limited to already elected representatives or party members, and you may not vote more than once.
c2-10: Freedom of expression is the right to write and say what you think. The right to vote is tied to a certain age, forming a government requires an election, and freedom of expression, on the contrary, means you don't have to agree with the majority.
c2-11: It is part of education because education in Sweden is built on democratic values. Students do not vote in real elections already in compulsory school, this is not an individual teacher's personal initiative outside the curriculum, and it is not a formal requirement for moving on to upper secondary school.
c2-12: Yes — starting a petition and writing opinion pieces in the media are lawful ways to have an influence. This right is not limited to politicians or party members, and petitions are not banned in Sweden.
c2-13: Yes — influencing your workplace through, for example, a trade union is one of several ways to take part in society. Union activity is not reserved for politicians, and there is no ban on combining it with political issues.
c2-14: The problem mentioned in connection with social media is that false information and hatred spread to create conflict in society. High voter turnout or too many parties are not real problems for democracy, and full state control over social media content is rather the opposite of how things actually work.
c2-15: This describes the problem that threats against people who take part in public debate can scare them away from participating. Journalists are allowed to criticize politicians as part of freedom of the press, journalists do not need to belong to a party, and writing about social issues in Swedish media has never been forbidden.
c2-16: For democracy to work well, it is important that many people can take part and have influence, that the information they receive is truthful, and that society protects those who take part in public debate. Limiting the right to speak to experts only, having everyone belong to one party, or holding elections as rarely as possible go against the very idea of democracy.
c2-17: This phenomenon is called segregation — people living apart depending on income or ethnic background. Integration describes the opposite situation, and the rule of law and freedom of expression are entirely different concepts unrelated to where people live.
c2-18: A consequence of segregation can be that people end up with unequal access to public services and culture, and that some areas are perceived as less safe. Segregation does not equalize incomes, does not reduce crime nationwide, and does not affect how seats in the Riksdag are distributed between parties.
c2-19: Segregation can reduce trust in public authorities and political engagement, which in turn can weaken democracy. It does not create new parties, is on the contrary clearly linked to democracy, and does not increase voter turnout — rather it decreases engagement.
c2-20: Politicians often propose language education and having different types of housing within one area. Building more areas with only one type of housing, on the contrary, reinforces segregation, and abolishing compulsory schooling or banning associations conflict with other important values.
c2-21: No — the laws in Sweden apply equally to everyone, regardless of financial standing. Neither a lighter penalty for the wealthy, a harsher one for the poor, nor any dependence on party affiliation is consistent with the principle of the rule of law.
c3-02: The Riksdag elects the Prime Minister, who then chooses their own ministers.
c3-03: It is submitted every autumn and shows the government's priorities.
c3-04: The Social Insurance Agency (Försäkringskassan) is responsible for social insurance, including parental benefit.
c3-05: JO and JK are special oversight bodies that check that other agencies act correctly.
c3-06: The regions are also responsible for public transport and county museums. Schools and elderly care are the municipality's responsibility.
c3-07: The municipal council (kommunfullmäktige) also appoints the members of the municipality's committees.
c3-08: The King is a symbol of the country, makes state visits, and receives heads of state from other countries.
c3-09: Next after Crown Princess Victoria is her daughter, Estelle, according to the line of succession set out in the Act of Succession (successionsordningen), one of the four fundamental laws.
c3-10: Rules that apply in all member states come from the European Union (EU) — EU countries cooperate and adopt laws that apply in all member states. The Nordic Council, the UN Security Council and the Council of Europe are also real organizations Sweden belongs to, but their decisions don't function the same way as binding legislation in all member states.
c3-11: The state (staten) consists of the Riksdag, the government, agencies and courts. That is more than just 'the Riksdag and the government', and it does not include municipalities and regions (which are separate levels) or the royal house (the King has no political power).
c3-12: Parliamentary representative democracy means that citizens vote in elections and elect representatives who then make decisions on their behalf — not that every law is put directly to a vote by all citizens, that the King appoints the members, or that only party leaders have the right to vote in the Riksdag.
c3-13: In a representative democracy, elected representatives make decisions on behalf of all voters between elections — not just those who voted for the winning party — and the law applies to everyone, regardless of whether that particular person voted or not. Refusing to pay tax out of disagreement with a law is illegal, and putting every law to a separate referendum would go against how representative democracy works.
c3-14: Before the vote, the governing parties and the opposition discuss and debate the proposal in the Riksdag. The King has no political power to decide the fate of laws, the opposition also has the right to speak, and courts do not approve bills — that is the Riksdag's own task.
c3-15: The Riksdag elects Sweden's Prime Minister, who is then tasked with forming a government. The King has no part in this decision — he has no political power — and there is neither a separate popular vote for Prime Minister nor a vote among the ministers themselves.
c3-16: The Budget Bill shows which policies the government wants to pursue and what the state should prioritize — it concerns the state's income and expenses, not Supreme Court decisions, election results, or the municipal tax rate, which municipalities set themselves.
c3-17: The opposition consists of the parties that do not support the government. The party with the most seats or the parties in government themselves are not automatically the opposition, and parties that did not enter the Riksdag do not take part in its work at all.
c3-18: The opposition's task is to scrutinize the government's work and propose alternative policies. Carrying out the government's decisions is the task of the government and its agencies, and appointing judges or deciding on new agencies are not part of the opposition's role.
c3-19: It is the Employment Agency (Arbetsförmedlingen) that helps people find work. The Tax Agency handles taxes, the Migration Agency handles residence permits and citizenship, and the police uphold law and order — none of them deals with job placement.
c3-20: Agencies must follow the law and the instructions they receive from the government — they do not act independently of the law, are not directly subordinate to each municipality's municipal council, and do not consult the King, who has no political power.
c3-21: The Parliamentary Ombudsman (JO) or the Chancellor of Justice (JK) can review an agency's actions in such cases. General courts such as the district court try criminal and civil cases, not general oversight of agencies, and neither the government nor the municipal council performs this oversight function.
c3-22: In the regional council (regionfullmäktige), decisions are made by politicians whom the region's residents themselves elected in the regional election — not officials appointed by the government, the region's municipal councils jointly, or the government directly.
c3-23: The regions also make sure there is public transport (buses, trams, metro) and are responsible for the county museums. The level of municipal tax is set by the municipalities themselves, building housing is not a regional task, and Riksdag members are elected, not appointed by the regions.
c3-24: The culture committee (kulturnämnden) is usually responsible for libraries. The education committee is responsible for schools, the social affairs committee for support and protection of residents, and the environment committee is not mentioned in connection with libraries.
c3-25: The members of the committees are elected by the municipal council (kommunfullmäktige) — not by the government, the regional council, or the residents directly in a separate election, which does not exist for this purpose.
c3-26: The municipality is responsible for everyday services such as water and sewage, and snow clearance. Healthcare at hospitals is run by the regions, foreign policy and defense by the state, and drafting the fundamental laws is the Riksdag's task.
c3-27: Sweden's largest municipality is Stockholm, the capital, home to almost a million people. Gothenburg and Malmö are also large cities, but less populous, while Dorotea in Västerbotten county is, on the contrary, the country's smallest municipality, with fewer than 3,000 residents.
c3-28: The King acts as a symbol for Sweden, makes state visits, and receives other countries' heads of state — but does not appoint ministers (that is done by the Prime Minister), does not enact laws (that is done by the Riksdag), and does not pass judgment in court (that is done by the courts), since he has no political power.
c3-29: No — the King has no political power and cannot stop a law decided by the Riksdag, whether at the government's request or during a certain time of year. This is a central part of Sweden being a constitutional monarchy.
c4-01: Elections to the Riksdag, regions and municipalities are held every fourth year, elections to the European Parliament every fifth.
c4-02: To vote in the Riksdag election you must be a Swedish citizen and at least 18 years old. For municipal and regional elections, Swedish citizenship is not required — three years of residence and registration are enough.
c4-03: A total of three years of residence and registration is required. Citizens of EU and Nordic countries only need to be registered as living in Sweden.
c4-04: Referendums in Sweden are advisory — politicians are not obliged to follow the result. For example, in the 2003 referendum on the euro, the people voted no, and although this was not a legal ban, Sweden kept the krona.
c4-05: The four-percent threshold exists to prevent too many parties from entering and to make stable majorities easier to form.
c4-06: Twenty percent of the votes gives roughly twenty percent of the seats. That is why parties often need to cooperate to form a majority.
c4-07: Eight parties: C, KD, L, MP, M, S, SD and V. Folkpartiet is the former name of Liberalerna.
c4-08: Elections to the Riksdag, regional council and municipal council are held every fourth year — all three at the same time. Elections to the European Parliament are held every fifth year, and there are no two-year or six-year cycles in the Swedish electoral system.
c4-09: No — to have the right to vote, you must have already turned 18. The age limit applies equally in all elections, so neither citizenship, registration, nor the type of election allows you to get around this requirement.
c4-10: For citizens of EU and Nordic countries, being registered as living in Sweden is enough — the three-year residence requirement applies to citizens of other countries. Swedish citizenship is not required for the municipal and regional elections, and the age limit everywhere is 18, not 21.
c4-11: EU citizens vote in the European Parliament election in the country where they are registered as living. The country of birth or the country that issued the passport play no role here, and you cannot freely choose which country to vote in either.
c4-12: Referendums in Sweden can be held nationally, in a region, or in a municipality. It is not true that they can only be held nationally or only in a municipality, and this is a domestic Swedish tool, not part of EU cooperation.
c4-13: In the 2003 referendum, the people voted no to replacing the krona with the euro, and Sweden kept the Swedish krona. The euro was never adopted in Sweden, the vote did take place, and the result was not a tie.
c4-14: You can vote in advance at specially designated locations. The right to vote is not lost, no one else may vote in your place, and voting is no longer possible after election day.
c4-15: You vote behind a screen because elections are secret and no one else should be able to see what choice you make. This has nothing to do with the speed of vote counting or the size of the premises, and parties checking how their members vote would directly contradict the principle of secret elections.
c4-16: In Sweden, you are free to start a new party together with others — that option is open to anyone. There is no obligation to choose among the existing parties, a blank vote is not the only way to express your position, and no permission from the Riksdag is required to form a party.
c4-17: Such parties pursue policy only for their own region or municipality, not at the national level. They have no seats in the Riksdag, there is no requirement to be present in at least ten municipalities, and parties being appointed by the government would go against democratic elections.
c5-01: The Instrument of Government (regeringsformen), the Freedom of the Press Act (tryckfrihetsförordningen), the Fundamental Law on Freedom of Expression (yttrandefrihetsgrundlagen), and the Act of Succession (successionsordningen).
c5-02: The Act of Succession (successionsordningen) is the fundamental law that regulates the line of succession.
c5-03: The Freedom of the Press Act protects specifically the printed form — books and newspapers. The Fundamental Law on Freedom of Expression concerns radio, TV and other forms of expression, and the Discrimination Act is not one of the fundamental laws at all.
c5-04: Freedom of expression protects the right to voice opinions, but certain statements are prohibited by law: defamation (förtal), incitement against an ethnic or national group (hets mot folkgrupp), and hate crimes (hatbrott).
c5-05: The right of public access (allemansrätten) is protected in the Instrument of Government (regeringsformen). You may not walk across a farmer's fields, enter someone else's garden, or litter.
c5-06: The police investigate, the prosecutor decides on charges, and the court passes judgment.
c5-07: The order of instances is: the district court (tingsrätt) → the court of appeal (hovrätt) → the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen).
c5-08: Remand detention (häktning) is decided by a court, and then the person can be held for a longer period.
c5-09: Lay judges (nämndemän) are appointed by the political parties and provide public insight into the judicial process.
c5-10: From age 15. In 2026 the government submitted a proposal to lower the age to 13 for serious crimes — but so far it remains a proposal.
c5-11: The Instrument of Government (regeringsformen) establishes that all public power in Sweden originates from the people — a basic principle of democracy, not from the monarch or a single body.
c5-12: This is a direct principle from the Instrument of Government (regeringsformen), which applies to everyone in Sweden, not only citizens.
c5-13: The Freedom of the Press Act (tryckfrihetsförordningen) covers the printed form (books, newspapers), while the Fundamental Law on Freedom of Expression (yttrandefrihetsgrundlagen) covers spoken and electronic forms: radio, TV.
c5-14: The right to vote in Riksdag elections requires Swedish citizenship, while the right to form associations and demonstrate applies to everyone living in the country.
c5-15: The right of public access (allemansrätten) allows picking berries, mushrooms and flowers on someone else's land regardless of who the owner is, as long as you are careful.
c5-16: The right of public access (allemansrätten) does not allow walking across cultivated fields, entering someone else's garden, or littering — these are the limits of the right, protecting the landowner's interests.
c5-17: Certain rare plants are protected separately — the general right to pick flowers (allemansrätten) does not extend to them.
c5-18: Freedom of the press and expression protects criticism of those in power and political opinions. What is forbidden is information that harms national security, such as military secrets.
c5-19: The Prison and Probation Service (Kriminalvården) is responsible for convicted persons and prisons, while the Crime Victim Authority (Brottsoffermyndigheten) is responsible specifically for those who have been victims of crime.
c5-20: Investigating at the crime scene is the police's task, deciding on charges is the prosecutor's task, and supporting victims is the Crime Victim Authority's (Brottsoffermyndigheten) task. The Prison and Probation Service (Kriminalvården) is responsible specifically for carrying out sentences.
c5-21: The independence of the courts is a key part of the rule of law (rättssäkerhet): political power cannot influence a specific verdict, though courts must, of course, still follow the law.
c5-22: The rule of law (rättssäkerhet) includes the right to a defense lawyer and the right to appeal — this guarantees that a decision can be reviewed.
c5-23: Cases begin in the district court (tingsrätten), and the court of appeal (hovrätten) is the second instance, hearing cases appealed from there.
c5-24: HD is not an automatic third instance for everyone: it selects only certain fundamentally important cases that have already gone through the first two instances.
c5-25: Custody disputes between parents count as civil cases (tvistemål), which are also handled by the district court (tingsrätten), not only criminal cases.
c5-26: The presumption of innocence means: a suspect is considered innocent until the court has issued a guilty verdict — regardless of what the prosecutor thinks.
c5-27: The police are responsible for order, prevention and investigation of crime. It is the courts, not the police, that pass judgment and decide on penalties.
c5-28: It is the police, not the Tax Agency or the Migration Agency, who issue passports and national ID cards to Swedish citizens.
c5-29: The police not only investigate crimes but also issue various permits, for example for a demonstration.
c5-30: The process begins when the person who was the victim of a crime reports it to the police. Only after that come questioning, the preliminary investigation, and possibly detention.
c5-31: These are two consecutive stages: first the police find out more about what happened (förhör), then a broader investigation follows, gathering evidence and talking to witnesses (förundersökning).
c5-32: After the police have arrested a person, it is a prosecutor (not a judge or a lay judge) who decides on detention (anhållan); a longer period in remand detention (häktning) is then decided by a court.
c5-33: Detention (anhållan, up to 72 hours) is decided by a prosecutor, while remand detention (häktning) for a longer period requires a court decision.
c5-34: The prosecutor's role during the trial is to prove the defendant's guilt. Defending the defendant is the defense lawyer's task, and the judge decides the penalty.
c5-35: The right to a defense includes the ability to challenge the prosecution's evidence and present your own — this is part of the rule of law (rättssäkerhet).
c5-36: If guilt is not proven, the court issues an acquittal — no automatic penalties or record entries follow.
c5-37: A child under 15 is not of the age of criminal responsibility (straffmyndig), so their case is handled not by a court or prosecutor, but by social services.
c5-38: The proposal concerns only serious crimes and the age of 13 — it is not yet a passed law, but specifically a 2026 proposal.
c5-39: The criminal record (belastningsregister) directly affects exactly such decisions as employment, obtaining a driving license, and citizenship.
c5-40: Neither the prosecutor, the lawyer, nor the police pass judgment — that is done by the judge, assisted in the district court by the lay judges.
c6-01: Thanks to this principle, journalists can request emails and other documents to examine how decisions were made.
c6-02: This is called source protection (meddelarskydd) and also includes the right to remain anonymous.
c6-03: Sveriges Radio, Sveriges Television, and Utbildningsradion. TV4 is a commercial channel.
c6-04: They are not allowed to earn money from advertising. The purpose is for everyone to have access to objective information regardless of where they live or how much money they have.
c6-05: The legally responsible publisher (ansvarig utgivare) must comply with laws that protect against defamation and insults.
c6-06: On social media, anyone can create content, and it is not verified in the same way as in other media.
c6-07: The state cannot decide or influence what is said in Swedish media — this is guaranteed by the fundamental laws on freedom of the press and freedom of expression. There is no pre-approval of news, public service companies must be independent of political interests, and the state does not set a list of allowed topics.
c6-08: The media inform about news, serve as a forum where people can freely discuss society, and are important for entertainment. Spreading official state information is not their task, selling advertising is only how some media fund themselves, and monitoring what citizens write is not part of the media's role at all.
c6-09: It is the principle of public access to official documents (offentlighetsprincipen) that gives this option: official documents from agencies are public and anyone can request them if they are not classified. Source protection concerns those who leak information to the media, the legally responsible publisher is accountable for what is published, and state support is a matter of funding, not access to documents.
c6-10: A classified document is not released — unlike official documents from agencies, which under the principle of public access are open to everyone. There is no requirement to publish it in a newspaper, no special access for foreign journalists, and no automatic declassification after three days.
c6-11: The state supports the media because it is important to have many different sources of news. The support does not give the state the right to control content, does not remove the requirement for a legally responsible publisher, and does not replace public service, which is funded differently.
c6-12: The journalist should verify the information with several independent sources and confirm they are reliable. Publishing based on a single unverified source, sending material to an agency for approval (which would violate freedom of the press), or waiting for competitors to publish first do not replace one's own fact-checking.
c6-13: Commercial channels earn income from selling advertising space or from people paying for access to a particular channel. The tax-collected fee funds public service, not commercial channels, they receive no grants from the Riksdag, and party membership fees have nothing to do with it.
c6-14: Yes — today most Swedish newspapers are also available online and update their news several times a day. The print form is not the only one, updating once a week is incorrect, and a subscription to the print edition is not required to read online.
c6-15: Public service companies must be independent of political and other interests and let different opinions be heard without taking sides. Following the government's line, only reporting positive news, or taking a side directly contradict the requirement of independence.
c6-16: On social media, anyone can create content, and that content is not controlled in the same way as in traditional media. The scrutiny there is weaker, not stricter, publishing is not limited to journalists, and the requirement for a legally responsible publisher does not apply to social media the way it does to newspapers, radio and TV.
c7-01: The declaration was adopted in 1948 and contains 30 articles. The UN was founded earlier, in 1945, by 51 countries — these two years are easy to mix up.
c7-02: Compliance is monitored by the Equality Ombudsman (Diskrimineringsombudsmannen, DO).
c7-03: This rule applies even when the people are married.
c7-04: The penalty targets the buyer, to signal that it is not acceptable to sexually exploit someone in exchange for payment.
c7-05: The Convention on the Rights of the Child (barnkonventionen) became Swedish law in 2020. Don't confuse it with 1979 (the ban on corporal punishment of children) or 2000 (recognition of national minorities) — different dates from the same chapter.
c7-06: In 2000, Sweden recognized official national minorities — Jews, Roma, Sámi, Sweden Finns, and Tornedalians. This is a separate date from 1979, when corporal punishment of children was banned, and from 2020, when the Convention on the Rights of the Child became Swedish law — these dates are easy to mix up.
c7-07: The five languages are Yiddish, Romani Chib, Sámi, Finnish, and Meänkieli.
c7-08: An advisory body on issues of language, culture and identity, which also has certain administrative functions.
c7-09: 1944 — decriminalization; 2003 — the right of same-sex couples to adopt; 2009 — the Church of Sweden allowed marriage.
c7-10: A hate crime motive is an aggravating circumstance.
c7-11: 51 countries created the UN in 1945 to prevent future wars and protect every person's rights. Today the UN has far more members (193), but it was 51 countries that founded the organization.
c7-12: The right to flee, seek asylum, and receive protection is listed directly among the rights in the UN declaration — it should not be confused with, for example, the right to vacation, which is also included but concerns something different.
c7-13: No one may be deprived of their citizenship without an approved and legitimate reason under the law — this is stated directly among the rights in the UN declaration, and criticizing the government is not such a reason. This protection applies to everyone, not just certain groups.
c7-14: The goal is equal rights, obligations, and equal influence over society and one's own life for women and men — not the dominance of one sex or a mechanical equal split in every profession, which is not mentioned in the chapter.
c7-15: Auditing workplaces plus the work of trade unions and agencies is the concrete mechanism from the chapter, not state-fixed wage levels or secret salaries, which are not mentioned there.
c7-16: It is specifically parental benefit (föräldrapenning) that allows both parents to stay home with the child, and the state actively encourages sharing this time — unlike child allowance (barnbidrag) or unemployment insurance (A-kassan), which serve other purposes.
c7-17: Being forced into marriage as a means of control by a family or group is specifically honor-based violence or oppression (hedersrelaterat våld/förtryck) — a distinct category, different from the general concept of intimate partner violence or hate crimes against a group.
c7-18: Honor-based violence (hedersrelaterat våld) does not only affect women and girls — the chapter explicitly states that boys, men, and LGBTQI people can also be victims, not only groups defined by age, citizenship, or profession.
c7-19: The permitted age for marriage is 18; marrying someone younger than that counts as child marriage (barnäktenskap) and is forbidden under Swedish law, regardless of whether anyone consented.
c7-20: It is specifically the Gender Equality Agency (Jämställdhetsmyndigheten) that is responsible for this particular task and funds, among other things, shelters and support organizations — unlike DO, which works on discrimination in general, not this specific topic.
c7-21: The purpose of the law is specifically to signal that sexually exploiting someone for money is unacceptable, not the technical convenience of proving guilt or the assumption that the seller is always coerced — this is not stated in the chapter as the reason.
c7-22: The Convention on the Rights of the Child (barnkonventionen) requires the court to ask for the child's own opinion in such a dispute, rather than automatically deciding based on a parent's income or referring the matter to another agency.
c7-23: The Convention on the Rights of the Child (barnkonventionen) explicitly requires municipalities to consider children's interests when building housing, playgrounds, and schools — not only cost, adults' preferences, or parking.
c7-24: 1979 is the year Sweden became the first country in the world to ban hitting children; 1948 is the year of the UN's Declaration of Human Rights, 2000 is the recognition of the national minorities, and 2020 is when the Convention on the Rights of the Child (barnkonventionen) became Swedish law. The dates are easy to mix up.
c7-25: The responsibility lies specifically with the parents or guardians, not with the school, the state directly, or the child — and the guardian is in turn entitled to support from society, for example from the municipality or healthcare.
c7-26: The chapter explicitly lists several forms of violence against children: besides physical abuse — psychological violence, sexual abuse, and female genital mutilation, not only school bullying or online violence.
c7-27: Sápmi stretches across four countries — Sweden, Norway, Finland, and Russia, not only Sweden and Norway or only northern Sweden.
c7-28: The right to practice reindeer husbandry is linked specifically to the Sami people's special status as a recognized indigenous people (urfolk) and their rights to land and resources in Sápmi — not a general right available to all Swedish residents, nor an EU or municipal decision.
c7-29: The right to use a minority language concerns specifically contacts with public authorities, preschool, and elderly care — not only communication at home or narrow specialized areas such as court or the Riksdag.
c7-30: The national minorities have lived in Sweden for a very long time and have their own languages and cultures, but precisely because of this they historically often lacked equal rights with the majority and were discriminated against — this is not about recent immigration or a lack of language.
c7-31: The Sami are, in addition to being a national minority, also Sweden's only recognized indigenous people (urfolk), which gives them additional rights beyond the national minority status also held by Jews, Roma, Sweden Finns, and Tornedalians.
c7-32: 2003 is the year same-sex couples gained the right to adopt; 1944 is the year homosexuality was decriminalized, and 2009 is the year the church allowed same-sex couples to marry. These dates are easy to mix up.
c7-33: 2009 is the year the Church of Sweden allowed same-sex couples to marry in church — a later and separate step from both the decriminalization of homosexuality (1944) and the right to adopt (2003).
c7-34: The right to marry a person of the same sex has been explicitly protected by Swedish law since 2009, and this is possible even in a church ceremony, not only a civil one. The right to adopt (2003) is a separate, earlier right and not a condition for marriage. Homosexuality was decriminalized in Sweden even earlier, in 1944.
c7-35: This concerns specifically laws against discrimination and laws that ensure equal participation in society, not benefits, working hours, or other topics unrelated directly to this part of the chapter.
c7-36: Discrimination in hiring based on disability is forbidden by law regardless of company size or whether it concerns the private or public sector.
c7-37: DO is an oversight agency that ensures the Discrimination Act is followed, not a court, a migration agency, or a body that sets wages — those tasks are performed by other bodies.
c7-38: DO is specifically the agency that handles cases of discrimination, including age discrimination — not debt collection, migration, or taxes.
c7-39: Workplaces, like schools, are required to actively work against discrimination themselves, not just report to the police or wait for DO to intervene from outside.
c7-40: A hate crime (hatbrott) is specifically a crime committed against a particular person because they belong to a group, and it carries a harsher penalty, while discrimination is a broader concept about treating people worse, which is not always a criminal offense with a hate motive.
c8-01: About 70% work in the private sector, and about 30% in the public sector, which is funded by taxes.
c8-02: The public sector is activities run by the state, the regions, and the municipalities: healthcare staff, teachers, childcare workers, police, and firefighters.
c8-03: The trade union confederations are LO (blue-collar workers), TCO (white-collar employees), and SACO (university-educated professionals). The other three options represent employers.
c8-04: Wages are set through negotiations between employers and trade unions, not by the state. Sweden has no legally mandated minimum wage.
c8-05: The unemployment insurance fund (A-kassan) is an economic association; the compensation is funded by the state and by membership fees.
c8-06: Debt restructuring (skuldsanering) means helping people with large debts get their finances in order.
c8-07: The amount of tax on work depends on income — the higher the salary, the higher the tax. Working without paying tax is illegal.
c8-08: About 30% of those working in Sweden work in the public sector, which is funded by taxes. The remaining roughly 70% work in the private sector; 10% and 50% are not accurate figures.
c8-09: A salon owned by a private individual belongs to the private sector — just like shops, restaurants, and other private companies. The public sector includes occupations funded by taxes, such as healthcare staff, teachers, and police officers; hairdressers still count as full employees, and a single occupation cannot belong to both sectors at once.
c8-10: Such industries are often located close to the natural resources they need. There is no law forbidding industry in big cities, industrial companies in Sweden are mostly private, not only municipal, and industrial workers are not required to live specifically in rural areas.
c8-11: The employer hires employees and pays their wages, while the employee performs the work in exchange for that pay — these are not the same concept, and the roles are not reversed. An employer in Sweden can be not only the state, but also a private company, a municipality, or a region.
c8-12: Employers in the private sector are represented by the Confederation of Swedish Enterprise (Svenskt näringsliv). LO represents employees, not employers, and Arbetsgivarverket and SKR also represent employers, but in the public sector, not the private one.
c8-13: The largest trade union confederations in Sweden are LO (blue-collar workers), TCO (white-collar employees), and SACO (university-educated professionals). Svenskt näringsliv, Arbetsgivarverket, and SKR are real organizations, but represent employers, not employees; government agencies and bodies of power do not belong to the labor market parties at all.
c8-14: The trade union negotiates wages with the employer and can help a member who has problems at work. Trade unions do not decide taxes, do not decide who to vote for, and do not replace the employee's employment relationship with the employer.
c8-15: A collective agreement is an agreement on wages and working conditions that applies to all employees at the workplaces covered by it, not only to whoever personally signed it. It is neither a law the Riksdag decides on nor an agreement between the state and an individual employee — wages in Sweden are set precisely by the labor market's parties through negotiation.
c8-16: In Sweden there are laws on working hours, the work environment, and vacation that protect the employee — the employer cannot freely set any conditions. A higher salary does not override these laws, and they apply equally in the private and public sectors.
c8-17: The employer must pay contributions to the state for the employees' pension and health insurance. The employee pays their own trade union membership fee, and private bank loans or municipal housing tax have nothing to do with the employer's obligations.
c8-18: Working without paying tax is illegal in Sweden — there are no exceptions based on income level, employer approval, or the first year of employment.
c8-19: Compensation from A-kassan is funded by the state and by members' membership fees. Employers' profits, municipal tax, and the EU budget are not directly connected to funding A-kassan.
c8-20: Personal finances cover a person's private income — for example wages or benefits — and expenses for things like housing, food, and clothing. This is broader than just money in a bank account or taxes paid, and has nothing to do with the state's own income and expenses.
c8-21: What the person should keep in mind is that the interest rate on this type of credit is often high. Credit cards are not free to use, the state does not automatically repay such debts, and paying by credit card in Sweden is entirely legal.
c8-22: The Enforcement Authority (Kronofogdemyndigheten) can help get finances in order through so-called debt restructuring (skuldsanering). The Tax Agency, the Migration Agency, and the Social Insurance Agency are real Swedish agencies, but none of them deals with resolving a family's debt situation.
c9-01: VAT (moms) is a value-added tax (mervärdesskatt). Employer contributions (arbetsgivaravgifter) are paid by the employer on top of employees' wages.
c9-02: The state also funds higher education and research. Healthcare is run by the regions, and schools and care by the municipalities.
c9-03: Elderly care (äldreomsorg) is the municipality's responsibility under Swedish law: help at home or moving to specially adapted housing.
c9-04: Social services (socialtjänsten) exist in every municipality: support, counseling, financial assistance, and protection.
c9-05: Primary care includes health centers, child health centers, and maternity clinics. Hospitals count as hospital care (sjukhusvård), while psychiatry, rehabilitation, and dental care fall under the 'other' (övrigt) category.
c9-06: Compulsory school (grundskola) in Sweden is for children between 6 and 16 years old. There are also upper secondary schools and municipal adult education (komvux).
c9-07: The welfare society means giving all residents basic economic and social security, for example through access to healthcare and education. The amount of tax paid does not determine access to public services, the state does not guarantee the same salary in every profession, and the right to support is not limited to citizens — it applies to all residents.
c9-08: A large part of the money for welfare comes from taxes. Loans from other countries, the EU budget, and fees for starting a business are not the main source of funding for the Swedish welfare system.
c9-09: Yes — tax in Sweden is paid not only by working individuals, but also by companies. It is not true that only private individuals or only state-owned companies pay tax, and there is no threshold of 100 employees for tax liability to apply.
c9-10: Income tax, VAT, and employer contributions, among others, help fund the Swedish welfare system. The other options name real types of fees and taxes that exist in various contexts, but not the three directly linked to funding Swedish welfare here.
c9-11: The employer pays employer contributions (arbetsgivaravgifter) to the state, part of which goes toward, among other things, employees' health insurance and pensions. VAT is paid when buying goods and services, the property fee has nothing to do with employees' wages, and the employee pays their own trade union membership fee, not the employer.
c9-12: The more people who work and the more goods and services that are bought and sold, the more money the state, the regions, and the municipalities receive for welfare. Claims that this has no effect at all, that the money automatically decreases, or that it only concerns municipal budgets are incorrect.
c9-13: Yes — some welfare services in Sweden are run by private companies, but they are still funded with tax money. It is not true that private companies are never funded with tax money, that this is only allowed in Stockholm, or that all care must be run by the region itself.
c9-14: The state also funds higher education and research at colleges and universities. Compulsory schools, preschools, after-school programs, and upper secondary schools are instead the municipalities' responsibility, not the state's direct responsibility.
c9-15: The regions collect tax from their own residents and use that money, among other things, to run hospitals and health centers. Loans from other countries, fees paid only by sick patients, and contributions from private insurance companies are not the main way regional healthcare is funded.
c9-16: Operations and advanced treatment count as hospital care (sjukhusvård), provided at emergency hospitals, county hospitals, and university hospitals. Primary care is provided at health centers, and social services and childcare do not belong to healthcare at all.
c9-17: Dental care and psychiatric care belong to the 'other' (övrigt) category, which also includes rehabilitation. Primary care and hospital care are other categories of healthcare, and childcare does not belong to healthcare at all.
c9-18: Each municipality decides for itself how high its municipal tax should be. The state does not set the same level for all municipalities, the region does not set the tax for the municipalities, and the EU makes no decisions about municipal tax in Sweden at all.
c9-19: The municipality is responsible for providing childcare spots, meaning preschools and after-school programs. The region is responsible for healthcare, the state funds other parts of welfare, and the employer is not obliged to provide a childcare spot.
c9-20: The municipality is responsible for upper secondary schools and municipal adult education, just as it is for compulsory schools. The region is responsible for healthcare, the state funds higher education at colleges and universities, and private companies with no connection to the public sector do not bear this responsibility.
c9-21: If staying at home is no longer working, the person can move to housing adapted for elderly people. The person does not need to move to another municipality, does not lose the right to continued help, and does not need to pay back help already given.
c10-01: More than a million Swedes emigrated to the USA between 1850 and 1920. Sweden was a poor country at the time: in the early 19th century the population was about 2.5 million, and a hundred years later it had doubled.
c10-02: The four largest were the labor movement (arbetarrörelsen), the free church movement (frikyrkorörelsen), the women's movement (kvinnorörelsen), and the temperance movement (nykterhetsrörelsen).
c10-03: The first such election was held in 1921, and Sweden thereby became a democracy. Before that came 1909 (the right to vote for almost all men) and 1918 (the decision on universal suffrage) — these dates are easy to mix up with 1921.
c10-04: It was signed in Saltsjöbaden near Stockholm between employers and trade unions.
c10-05: Per Albin Hansson, the Social Democrats' leader at the time, formulated the idea of folkhemmet in 1928. Gustav V was the reigning king at the time but had nothing to do with the idea, and Gustav Vasa lived four centuries earlier.
c10-06: The event shook Sweden and showed how deep the conflicts between employers and workers were.
c10-07: Raoul Wallenberg issued protective passports to Jews, saving them from deportation to concentration camps. In addition, Sweden received about 7,000 Danish Jews, and the Red Cross transported people out of the camps using the 'White Buses'.
c10-08: The Social Democrats were most often in power from 1945 to 1976; a 40-hour work week and five weeks of paid vacation were introduced.
c10-09: The rapid movement of people into the cities created a housing shortage; new residential areas grew up in the suburbs.
c10-10: The reform reflected a move toward a more equal society.
c10-11: 200 years ago almost the entire population lived in the countryside and farmed the land; compared with other European countries, Sweden was poor.
c10-12: More efficient agriculture provided more food, and medical advances reduced child mortality — together these doubled the population in about a century.
c10-13: More than a million Swedes emigrated to the USA between 1850 and 1920, precisely because of poverty and a lack of work at home.
c10-14: Sweden's industrialization began with sawmills producing timber products and steel-manufacturing industries; the car and IT industries came much later.
c10-15: This is the classic division of power by estate in pre-reform Sweden — the king and representatives of the old estates: nobility, clergy, merchants, and peasantry.
c10-16: 1809 is the earliest of the reform dates on the path to democracy: limiting the King's power. The other dates belong to later stages: 1865 the representation reform, 1909 voting rights for men, 1918 the decision on universal suffrage.
c10-17: 1865 is the Riksdag representation reform, when the old estate privileges of the nobility and clergy were abolished. This is later than 1809 (limiting the King's power), but earlier than 1909 and 1918 (expanded voting rights) and 1921 (the first election with women voting).
c10-18: The 1865 reform removed the old estate privileges but did not give women or poor men the right to vote — meanwhile the wealthiest had several votes.
c10-19: The popular movements of the 1800s fought for concrete political and labor rights — an eight-hour workday, the right to vote, and religious freedom.
c10-20: Despite their radical demands, the movements acted within the law: demonstrations, protest meetings, books, and press articles — not violence.
c10-21: 1909 concerns almost all men, but not yet women. Full universal suffrage was decided later, in 1918, and the first election with women voting was held in 1921.
c10-22: 1918 is the decision on full universal suffrage (including women), but in practice women first voted in a Riksdag election only in 1921. Don't confuse it with 1909, when almost all men gained the right to vote.
c10-23: The order is: 1865 (the nobility and clergy lose influence) → 1918 (the decision on universal suffrage) → 1921 (the first election with women) → 1931 (Ådalen).
c10-24: Just as it later did during World War II, Sweden declared itself neutral in World War I, although this did not spare the country from the war's consequences.
c10-25: Neutrality did not protect Sweden from the economic consequences of the war — a shortage of goods sparked public discontent and protests.
c10-26: The democratic breakthrough of 1921 did not immediately solve economic problems — unemployment and class inequality remained a source of conflicts and strikes.
c10-27: The key idea of the Swedish model is negotiation directly between employers and trade unions, through collective agreements, without state involvement.
c10-28: These are the same groups that were later, in 2000, officially recognized as Sweden's national minorities — but in the 1930s they became victims of discriminatory pseudoscience.
c10-29: This is a dark side of modernization: people who did not fit into society due to their health were isolated — Sweden has only recently acknowledged this and provided some of those affected with compensation.
c10-30: To reduce the risk of being drawn into the war, the Swedish government allowed German troop transit — a compromise on neutrality that is still debated today.
c10-31: The 'White Buses' operation was carried out specifically by the Red Cross. The UN and NATO were only formed after the war and could not have taken part.
c10-32: The Social Democrats enjoyed strong voter support and governed almost continuously on their own throughout these three decades.
c10-33: It was precisely these specific conditions — a 40-hour week with Saturdays off and five weeks of fully paid vacation — that became a symbol of the record years.
c10-34: During the record years, many people came to work in Sweden specifically from Finland, Greece, Yugoslavia, and Turkey — the main countries of labor migration in that period.
c10-35: The cause was not suffrage, the Saltsjöbaden Agreement, or the million programme themselves (real events from the same period) — it was the labor shortage in a fast-growing economy: demand for labor outstripped the domestic supply, and Sweden began actively recruiting workers from abroad.
c10-36: It was specifically the television set that was the novelty of the early 1960s. Radio already existed earlier, while the internet and mobile phone came much later.
c10-37: Rapid technological development meant that knowledge acquired became outdated faster than before — hence the growing importance of lifelong and adult education.
c10-38: After decades of Social Democratic rule (1945–1976), the economic crisis of the mid-1970s led to a change of power in 1976 — the start of a period of alternating governments.
c10-39: From the 1980s, attention to the rights and choices of the individual grew stronger — this was reflected, among other things, in the ability to choose one's school and healthcare provider.
c10-40: The digital revolution is the change that began specifically in the 1990s and continues today, including AI. Industrialization, on the other hand, dates to the 1800s.
c11-01: Sweden joined the EU in 1995. Don't confuse it with 1949 (the founding of the Council of Europe), 1991 (the collapse of the USSR, which changed the situation in Europe), or 2003 (the referendum on the euro) — these dates concern other events from the same chapter. 2022 and 2024 are the years of the NATO application and NATO membership, even later events.
c11-02: The EU's four freedoms are the ability to study, move, work, and sell goods freely between countries. Cooperation within the EU began after World War II to create peace and stability in Europe.
c11-03: The European Court of Human Rights operates within the Council of Europe, which was founded in 1949 and works on human rights, democracy, and the rule of law.
c11-04: The Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida) supports the development of democracy, equality, and the economy in other countries.
c11-05: Sweden lost Finland, which had been part of the country for almost 700 years. Norway is a different story: it was drawn into a union with Sweden later and became independent peacefully only in 1905.
c11-06: Sweden and Finland applied almost simultaneously after Russia's attack on Ukraine in 2022; Sweden became a member in 2024. Don't confuse it with 1995 (Sweden joining the EU), 2003 (the euro referendum), or 1949 (the founding of the Council of Europe) — these are all other organizations and dates.
c11-07: General military conscription (värnplikt) is something different: it covers men and women who have turned 18.
c11-08: Sweden mainly cooperates with the other Nordic countries through the Nordic Council and the Nordic Council of Ministers — both bodies agree on matters that each country then implements. The European Union, the Council of Europe, UN bodies, and the Swedish Armed Forces and Sida are also real parts of Sweden's international cooperation, but do not specifically concern Nordic cooperation.
c11-09: The EU countries cooperate in many areas — agriculture, the economy, the environment, trade, and migration. A joint currency does not apply to all EU countries (Sweden, for example, kept the krona), military defense is NATO's task, and Sida is a separate Swedish agency for international development cooperation, not part of EU cooperation itself.
c11-10: It is specifically the EU's four freedoms that give citizens of member states the right to freely study, move, work, and sell goods in other EU countries without a special permit. The Council of Europe deals with human rights and democracy, NATO with military defense, and the Nordic Council with cooperation within Norden, not the whole EU.
c11-11: The Council of Europe was founded in 1949 and works for human rights, democracy, and the rule of law. 1995 is the year Sweden joined the EU, 1945 is the year the UN was founded, and 2024 is the year Sweden joined NATO — these dates and organizations are easy to mix up.
c11-12: The UN was founded in 1945, and almost all the world's countries are members. 1949 is the year the Council of Europe was founded, 1995 is the year Sweden joined the EU, and 2024 is the year Sweden joined NATO — these organizations have far fewer members than the UN.
c11-13: One of the UN's main purposes is to preserve peace and security in the world and work for human rights. Overseeing member states' economies and currencies is not the UN's task, coordinating military defense under a joint commander resembles more the function of a military alliance like NATO, and EU agricultural aid is distributed by the EU itself, not the UN.
c11-14: Through Sida, Sweden supports other countries in developing democracy, equality, the economy, and a sustainable society. Sida does not grant EU membership (EU countries decide that themselves), does not build up other countries' military forces, and does not require the adoption of Swedish laws — these are not the development agency's tasks.
c11-15: What is special about Sweden is that it has had peace for a very long, unbroken period — since the early 1800s — making it one of the few countries in the world with such a long peace period. The claim that Sweden has never been at war at all is incorrect (its last war was precisely in the early 1800s), Sweden joined NATO only in 2024, not right after World War II, and it has gone to war less often, not more, than most European countries.
c11-16: As a result of the Napoleonic Wars, Norway was forced into a union with Sweden. Norway did not conquer any territory from Sweden, joined NATO much later and separately from Sweden (already in 1949), and although Norway had been linked to Denmark before the union with Sweden, it did not reunite with Denmark during this period — instead it entered a new union, with Sweden.
c11-17: Norway became independent peacefully in 1905, without war. There was no war between Sweden and Norway over this, the dissolution has nothing to do with World War I in 1918, and the union itself has long ceased to exist — Norway has been independent for over a century.
c11-18: The Cold War was a conflict between a Western bloc led by the USA and an Eastern bloc led by the Soviet Union. There was no open war between Sweden and the USSR, the EU in its current form did not yet unite all European countries the way it does today, and there was never any alliance between Norden and the USSR.
c11-19: Sweden remained neutral and stayed outside NATO during the Cold War — unlike Denmark and Norway. It joined neither NATO nor the USSR's alliance, and did not form a separate defense alliance with Finland during that period either — the two countries submitted a joint NATO application much later, in 2022.
c11-20: Sweden applied for NATO membership because of growing concern about security in Norden after Russia's attack on Ukraine in 2022. The euro referendum was in 2003 and has nothing to do with NATO, the EU does not require member states to join NATO, and the Cold War had long since ended by 2022, not just broken out.
c11-21: Total defense duty (totalförsvarsplikt) can cover anyone living in Sweden aged between 16 and 70 — citizenship is not required, and a 65-year-old still falls within that range. Having military training is not a condition either.
c11-22: General military conscription in Sweden covers all men and women who have turned 18 — not only men as it did before, and not only people already serving in the Armed Forces. The 16–20 age range belongs to a different concept — total defense duty (totalförsvarsplikt) starts at age 16, not military conscription (värnplikt).
c11-23: After the tests, it is decided who becomes eligible for basic military training, but in practice only some of them go on to complete it. There is no immediate mandatory service for everyone, no automatic lifelong exemption, and no automatic assignment to the navy without selection.
c11-24: The Swedish Armed Forces (Försvarsmakten) consist of the army, the navy, and the air force. The police, the Coast Guard, and Swedish Customs are real Swedish agencies, but are not part of the Armed Forces; a joint NATO force is not the same as Sweden's national armed forces, and the government and the Riksdag's defense committee make political decisions but are not part of the armed forces' structure.
c11-25: It is specifically the Armed Forces (Försvarsmakten) that can take part in international operations, in addition to protecting Sweden's territory. Civil defense concerns keeping society functioning within the country, the Nordic Council is a cooperation body, not a military structure, and the police are responsible for law and order, not international military operations.
c11-26: Civil defense means that activities such as school, work, and healthcare should be able to keep functioning during war or crisis. This complements rather than replaces the work of the Armed Forces, evacuating the population abroad is not described as part of civil defense, and civilian agencies are not shut down during war — on the contrary, they are meant to keep functioning.
c11-27: This concerns civil defense — it is civil defense specifically that is responsible for making sure schools, work, and healthcare keep functioning during a crisis or war. This is not the task of the Armed Forces, NATO's joint forces, or the Nordic Council of Ministers, which deal with other matters.
c12-01: The state guarantees everyone the right to decide for themselves whether to belong to a particular religion.
c12-02: The Freedom of Religion Act, which made it possible to freely choose any religion or none at all, was passed in 1951. Even earlier, in 1860, it became allowed to leave the Church of Sweden, but only when joining another Christian community — an earlier and more limited step. In 2000 the state and the church were fully separated — a later, independent step.
c12-03: The state and the Church of Sweden were separated in 2000. After that, the church became one of many faith communities, although it remains the largest Christian community in the country. 1860 is the earlier date when it first became allowed to leave the Church of Sweden by joining another Christian community, and 1951 is the year the Freedom of Religion Act was introduced — these dates are easy to mix up with the church-state separation in 2000.
c12-04: The Church of Sweden has about five million members. It is the country's largest religious community, although its membership is gradually declining.
c12-05: The number of Muslims grew through immigration after World War II; the first mosques were built in the 1970s.
c12-06: The history of Judaism in Sweden can be traced back to the 1700s. That was when Jews first gained the right to live and practice their religion in Sweden; full civil rights came only in 1870.
c12-07: Yes — everyone in Sweden has the right to freely choose their faith or to have no faith at all; this is a direct expression of freedom of religion. There is no obligation to belong to a faith community, no requirement to report it annually to the Tax Agency, and no restriction of this right to members of the Church of Sweden only.
c12-08: This first became allowed in 1860, but only on condition of joining another Christian community. The 1700s is the period Judaism's history in Sweden dates from, 1951 is when the Freedom of Religion Act was passed, and 2000 is when the Church of Sweden was separated from the state — these dates are easy to mix up.
c12-09: The Instrument of Government (regeringsformen) establishes that everyone has the right to practice their religion and that no one may be discriminated against because of their faith. The law does not require citizens to belong to a Christian community, does not restrict voting rights based on religion, and does not forbid religious communities from accepting new members.
c12-10: The goal of the subject is to provide a broad understanding of different religions and worldviews and to promote tolerance and respect. Teaching that Christianity is 'the only correct religion,' preparing for baptism, or trying to convince students not to believe at all would all contradict the subject's neutral purpose.
c12-11: Yes — many people in Sweden celebrate Christian holidays as part of their cultural heritage, even though they are not religious believers. There is no restriction to Church of Sweden members, no ban on celebrating without being a believer, and no requirement to be baptized first.
c12-12: Rituals such as baptism, church weddings, and Christian funerals are still common, even among those who do not describe themselves as believers. Daily prayers and fasting during Ramadan belong to Islamic practice, not the Swedish Christian rituals referred to here.
c12-13: Religious diversity has increased because immigration has grown, and with it the range of religions practiced in the country. The state does not require anyone to choose a new religion, the Church of Sweden has not split into new communities, and Sweden's population has not declined — on the contrary, it has grown.
c12-14: The three main branches of Christianity are Orthodox churches, the Catholic Church, and Protestant churches. Sunni, Shia, and Sufism belong to Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Judaism are entirely different world religions, and the combination 'Lutheranism, Islam, and Judaism' mixes one Christian branch with two other religions.
c12-15: The Church of Sweden's historical roots are in the Lutheran, Protestant tradition, established in the 1500s. The Orthodox tradition has no connection to the Church of Sweden, Sweden was Catholic only before this shift in the 1500s, not today, and Islam is an entirely different religion.
c12-16: During the Middle Ages, before the shift to the Lutheran tradition in the 1500s, Sweden was a Catholic country — which is why so many medieval churches remain across the country. Sweden has never been a Muslim or Buddhist country, and the claim that it had no religion at all during the Middle Ages is incorrect.
c12-17: Jews gained full civil rights in 1870. 1860 is the year Swedes were first allowed to leave the Church of Sweden, 1951 is the year the Freedom of Religion Act was passed, and 2000 is the year the Church of Sweden was separated from the state — these dates are easy to mix up.
c12-18: Contacts with Hinduism and Buddhism began mainly in the 1900s, partly through travel to Asia and growing interest in meditation and yoga. The 1700s belongs to the history of Judaism in Sweden, the 1500s to the shift to the Lutheran tradition, and these religions have been present in Sweden long before the 2000s.
c12-19: The number of Muslims in Sweden grew through immigration after World War II, and the first mosques were built in the 1970s. In the 1800s there were hardly any Muslims in Sweden, medieval churches were not demolished to make way for mosques, and none of Sweden's four fundamental laws concerns a 'protected religion'.
c12-20: Branches such as Sunni and Shia are represented among Sweden's Muslim congregations. Orthodox and Catholic are Christian branches, Lutheran and Reformed also belong to Christianity, and Hinduism and Buddhism are entirely different world religions.
c12-21: Religious congregations offer a sense of community and help preserve and promote the tradition and culture of their religion. They do not set their own laws in place of Swedish law (Sweden is a secular state with a single law for everyone), do not collect taxes on the state's behalf, and do not replace the municipality's social services.
c13-01: In the evening large bonfires are lit and traditional spring songs are sung to welcome spring.
c13-02: It is a public holiday; the labor movement holds demonstrations across the country.
c13-03: June 6 became a paid public holiday in 2005 by decision of the Riksdag. The date was chosen because of two earlier events: on June 6, 1523, Gustav Vasa was elected king, and on June 6, 1809, a new Instrument of Government was adopted.
c13-04: The tradition dates from before Christianity. Typical food includes herring, new potatoes, and strawberries.
c13-05: On this day, saffron buns (lussebullar) are traditionally served.
c13-06: The main family celebration takes place on Christmas Eve (julafton), December 24.
c13-07: Eid al-Fitr is the holiday that marks the end of the fasting month of Ramadan. Nowruz and its Kurdish variant Newroz are the Persian and Kurdish New Year, celebrated on the spring equinox, March 21, and are not connected to Ramadan.
c13-08: Traditions change as society develops — the holidays have not changed names or stopped being Christian in origin, the Church of Sweden has never banned anything of the sort (in 2000 the church was only separated from the state), and religious celebration is not limited to any single group in the population.
c13-09: New Year's Eve is celebrated in Sweden, just as in many places around the world, with parties, dinners, and fireworks at midnight. Eggs, lamb, and herring are Easter food, wreaths and dancing around a pole are part of Midsummer, and julotta is the Christmas morning service — all other holidays of the year.
c13-10: Easter commemorates the death of Jesus on Good Friday and his resurrection on Easter Sunday. The birth of Jesus is celebrated at Christmas, Saint Lucia and the light amid the winter darkness on Saint Lucia's Day, and the memory of deceased relatives on All Saints' Day — other holidays during the year.
c13-11: On Easter Saturday it is common to eat eggs, lamb, salmon, and herring. Herring with new potatoes and strawberries is Midsummer food, saffron buns are the treat for Saint Lucia's Day, and Christmas food is served on Christmas Eve — other holidays.
c13-12: On Walpurgis Night, people traditionally light large bonfires and sing spring songs to welcome spring. Wreaths and dancing around a pole are part of Midsummer, candles on graves are an All Saints' Day tradition, and opening a window on a calendar is part of Advent — other holidays.
c13-13: At the May 1 demonstrations, people from trade unions, political parties, and other groups usually give speeches. The Church of Sweden, the royal family, and the Armed Forces are real Swedish institutions, but are not connected to the labor movement's May Day demonstrations.
c13-14: June 6 is Sweden's National Day, and it is on this day that many municipalities hold ceremonies to welcome new citizens of the country. Walpurgis Night, Midsummer Eve, and May 1 are other holidays celebrated on different dates.
c13-15: Midsummer is an old tradition dating from before Christianity came to Sweden. It was June 6 (National Day) that became a public holiday by a Riksdag decision in 2005, examples of traditions that came with immigrants are Nowruz and Eid al-Fitr, and it is Easter that commemorates Jesus's resurrection — other holidays or events.
c13-16: On Midsummer Eve, people often weave flower wreaths and dance around a maypole. Bonfires and speeches about spring are a Walpurgis Night tradition, opening a window on a calendar is part of Advent, and lighting candles on graves is done on All Saints' Day — other holidays.
c13-17: Lighting candles on graves on a Saturday in late October or early November is a tradition belonging to All Saints' Day. Midsummer Eve, May 1, and New Year's Eve are other holidays, celebrated differently and at different times of year.
c13-18: Advent means arrival and is a period of preparation before Christmas — the four Sundays before Christmas Day. Light and Saint Lucia belong to Saint Lucia's Day, resurrection to Easter, and Swedish independence to National Day — other concepts and holidays.
c13-19: A procession with a crown of candles on the head and special songs is the Lucia celebration. Julotta is the Christmas morning service, the Advent celebration is the waiting period before Christmas, and Walpurgis Night is celebrated with bonfires and spring songs — other traditions.
c13-20: On Christmas Eve, many families in Sweden gather to spend time together, eat Christmas food, and give each other Christmas presents. Bonfires and speeches about spring belong to Walpurgis Night, candles on graves to All Saints' Day, and the Lucia procession takes place on December 13 — other dates and holidays.
c13-21: Today, Christmas has become, for many Swedes, a family tradition without religious meaning. The Church of Sweden does not require anyone to celebrate Christmas and does not require membership (since 2000 the church has been separated from the state), and the holiday's name and meaning have not changed.
c13-22: Along with Eid al-Fitr, the Persian New Year Nowruz and the Kurdish New Year Newroz, for example, came to Sweden with immigrants, celebrated on the spring equinox. Midsummer, Walpurgis Night, Christmas, Easter, All Saints' Day, and May 1 are old Swedish traditions, not holidays that came with immigrants.
